problems.stem: A club survey has 8 respondents. One row reads: 'Age 19, Major Nursing, Dorm Hall B, Works at campus library front desk'. Why is this row a privacy concern even without a name column?
options: It is fine because the name was removed.
The combination of major, dorm, and job is specific enough to re-identify one person in a small group.
It is a concern only if an email address is present.
Eight rows is too few to ever be a privacy concern.
problems.explanation: Removing the name is not enough. A combination of quasi-identifiers (major, dorm, specific job) can single out one person, especially in a small dataset.

problems.stem: Your dataset has 6 students. You make a chart titled 'Average GPA by gender' where one group has only 1 person. What is the ethical problem with publishing that bar?
options: The bar will be the wrong color.
An average over a group of 1 both exposes that individual's exact value and presents a single point as a reliable group pattern.
Averages cannot be computed for one person.
The chart should use a pie chart instead.
problems.explanation: A group of one is not anonymous and not a pattern. The 'average' is just that person's value, and presenting it as a group trend is both a privacy and an honesty problem. Suppress or combine tiny groups.

problems.stem: You want an AI tool to help summarize a small dataset that contains classmates' names and email addresses. What is the responsible step before pasting it in?
options: Paste the whole sheet because the tool is private.
Remove or mask the direct identifiers (names, emails) first, since you should not share others' personal data with a third-party tool.
Paste only the names so the tool can label rows.
Add more personal detail so the summary is accurate.
problems.explanation: Sharing classmates' names and emails with an external tool exposes their data without consent. 'The tool is private' is not a safe assumption: as of 2026, consumer AI chat tools (such as the free or personal tiers of ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini) may retain pasted text and use it for model training by default unless you opt out in settings, while enterprise or institution-licensed tiers typically do not train on submitted content by default. Strip or mask direct identifiers before pasting, regardless of which tool or tier you use.

problems.stem: From a survey of 7 people, 4 chose option A. Which reporting choice is the most honest?
options: Report '57% of respondents chose A' with no mention of the sample size.
Report '4 of 7 respondents chose A' so the reader sees how small the sample is.
Report 'a majority of people prefer A' as a general claim.
Report 'most users choose A' to sound more confident.
problems.explanation: With a tiny sample, a raw count like '4 of 7' is more honest than a percentage that hides how few responses there were. Percentages on small n can mislead.
